## Business question

Which customers are most likely to stop purchasing in the next 90 days, and how
can marketing prioritize a practical retention audience? This example uses
fully synthetic retail customer data. Its hidden persona labels support
simulation checks and are excluded from both segmentation inputs and the churn
prediction features.

## 1. Create and inspect the mock marketing data

```{r data}
customers <- load_customers()
dim(customers)
head(customers)
summary(customers[c("age", "tenure_months", "recency_days", "frequency_12m",
                    "monetary_12m", "discount_usage_rate", "nps_score",
                    "churned_90d")])
```

The table combines customer attributes, purchasing history, digital-channel
activity, email engagement, service contacts, campaign response, and a
simulated 90-day churn outcome. The churn event is generated from the observed
historical risk signals, plus unobserved individual variation and a source
persona effect.

```{r persona-check}
persona_summary <- aggregate(
  cbind(recency_days, frequency_12m, monetary_12m, churned_90d,
        responded_campaign) ~ true_persona,
  data = customers, FUN = mean
)
persona_summary
```

## 2. RFM baseline

Rank-based quintiles make the RFM scores robust to ties. Recency is reversed so
that a high R score means a more recent purchase.

```{r rfm}
customers <- cbind(customers, rfm_scores(customers))
customers$rfm_segment <- cut(
  customers$rfm_score,
  breaks = c(2, 6, 9, 12, 15),
  labels = c("Low", "Developing", "Strong", "Top"),
  include.lowest = TRUE
)
aggregate(churned_90d ~ rfm_segment, customers, mean)
```

RFM gives a useful, explainable baseline, but it cannot distinguish channel
preferences, campaign responsiveness, and other behaviors that may be useful
for customer strategy.

## 3. Behavioral segmentation

Segments use purchase recency, frequency, order value, discount usage, digital
activity, email engagement, service contacts, and NPS. Skewed measures are
log-transformed and all inputs standardized. Churn outcomes and hidden personas
are deliberately excluded.

```{r segment}
customers <- fit_segments(customers, k = 5, seed = 42)
table(customers$segment)
```

```{r segment-profile}
profiles <- segment_profile(customers)
profiles
```

```{r segment-plot}
ggplot(profiles, aes(x = reorder(segment, churn_rate), y = churn_rate, fill = segment)) +
  geom_col(show.legend = FALSE) +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent_format()) +
  labs(title = "Observed 90-day churn rate by behavioral segment",
       x = NULL, y = "Churn rate") +
  theme_minimal()
```

The segment labels are initially numeric. Profile their typical activity,
revenue, campaign response, and churn rate before assigning business names or
choosing segment-specific actions.

## 4. Train churn prediction models

The holdout is stratified by the churn outcome. Logistic regression provides an
interpretable baseline; a random forest can capture nonlinear behavior and
interactions. The model uses information available before the prediction
horizon. It does not use `churned_90d` or the hidden persona as a feature.

```{r fit-models, cache=TRUE}
if (!requireNamespace("ranger", quietly = TRUE)) {
  stop("Install the ranger package to fit the random-forest model.")
}
model_fit <- train_churn_models(customers, test_fraction = 0.25, seed = 42)
model_metrics <- data.frame(
  model = names(model_fit$models),
  holdout_auc = vapply(model_fit$models, `[[`, numeric(1), "auc")
)
classification <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(model_fit$models), function(name) {
  cbind(
    model = name,
    classification_metrics(model_fit$truth, model_fit$models[[name]]$scores)
  )
}))
model_metrics
classification
```

```{r importance}
head(model_fit$models[["Random forest"]]$importance, 15)
```

```{r roc-plot}
roc_points <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(model_fit$models), function(name) {
  scores <- model_fit$models[[name]]$scores
  thresholds <- sort(unique(c(Inf, scores, -Inf)), decreasing = TRUE)
  data.frame(
    model = name,
    fpr = vapply(thresholds, function(t) mean(scores[model_fit$truth == 0] >= t),
                 numeric(1)),
    tpr = vapply(thresholds, function(t) mean(scores[model_fit$truth == 1] >= t),
                 numeric(1))
  )
}))
ggplot(roc_points, aes(fpr, tpr, colour = model)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") +
  coord_equal() +
  labs(title = "Holdout ROC curves", x = "False positive rate",
       y = "True positive rate", colour = "Model") +
  theme_minimal()
```

## 5. Retention targeting

Scores are evaluated by their ability to rank future churners ahead of other
customers. A top-quintile targeting rule is an illustrative budget constraint,
not a universally optimal choice.

```{r targeting}
forest_scores <- model_fit$models[["Random forest"]]$scores
deciles <- churn_deciles(model_fit$truth, forest_scores)
deciles
top_quintile_metrics <- top_fraction_metrics(model_fit$truth, forest_scores, 0.2)
top_quintile_metrics
```

```{r lift-plot}
ggplot(deciles, aes(x = decile, y = lift)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#2a78d6") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey35") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = deciles$decile) +
  labs(title = "Churn lift by risk decile", x = "Highest-risk decile first",
       y = "Lift over average churn rate") +
  theme_minimal()
```

```{r score-customers}
customers$churn_probability <- predict_churn(model_fit, customers)
head(customers[order(-customers$churn_probability),
               c("customer_id", "segment", "churn_probability",
                 "recency_days", "frequency_12m", "nps_score")], 10)
```

## 6. Recommended interpretation

- Validate probability calibration and ranking on a later time period before
  activating a retention audience.
- Compare campaign cost, contact capacity, customer value, and intervention
  effectiveness; a high churn probability alone does not mean an offer will
  prevent churn.
- Test interventions using randomized holdouts and measure incremental
  retention rather than treating predicted risk as causal evidence.
- Monitor model performance and representation across relevant customer groups.

## 7. Save reproducible outputs

```{r export}
dir.create(file.path("data", "processed"), recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
dir.create("reports", recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
utils::write.csv(
  customers[c("customer_id", "segment", "R", "F", "M", "churn_probability")],
  file.path("data", "processed", "customer_churn_scores.csv"),
  row.names = FALSE
)
utils::write.csv(profiles, file.path("reports", "segment_profiles.csv"),
                 row.names = FALSE)
utils::write.csv(deciles, file.path("reports", "churn_deciles.csv"),
                 row.names = FALSE)
utils::write.csv(model_metrics, file.path("reports", "model_metrics.csv"),
                 row.names = FALSE)
utils::write.csv(
  classification, file.path("reports", "classification_metrics.csv"),
  row.names = FALSE
)
message("Saved scored customers, segment profiles, deciles, and model metrics.")
```
